Transformer Regulation, Efficiency and Three-Phase Transformers (Ch3)

Why this matters in the exam: Q2 of every final is “Magnetic Circuits and Transformers” (20 marks), and the transformer part always uses the simplified equivalent circuit. Jun24 Q2c (8 marks) is a three-phase transformer open-circuit calculation plus “by what factor does it change if V is halved”. Jun24 Q4c(ii) (3 marks) asks you to explain transformer losses and how they vary with output. Jun23 Q2c (6 marks) is the KVL equation . The 2023 quiz Q5 to Q7 (18 of 40 marks) and the 2024 test Q6 and Q7 are all built on the same three tools: , and .

1. The core ideas

Everything in this pack uses the simplified equivalent circuit referred to the primary, per phase (lecture 3.9.5). The shunt branch sits across the input terminals (). The series branch carries the referred load current . Here and .

Open-circuit (OC) behaviour. With the input sees only . Then , and . With the model’s constant and , halving gives: current , P , Q , pf .

Why the OC current is not zero. The core has finite permeability, so it needs an mmf (the magnetising current through ) to set up the flux. The core also has hysteresis and eddy-current losses, and these need a real current (through ). Saturation makes the magnetising current rise much faster than the voltage near rated flux. Your Prac 2 data shows this clearly: fell from 3982 Ω at 100 V to 366 Ω at 240 V.

2. The method

Recognise the question type:

  • “delivering … at a pf of … at rated output voltage” → Type A (load analysis, which leads to and regulation).
  • “copper loss / iron loss / efficiency” → Type B.
  • “at what load is efficiency a maximum” → Type C.
  • “open-circuit … rated input voltage … if the voltage was halved” → Type D.
  • “explain the losses / why is the no-load current not zero” → Type E (words only).

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Adding magnitudes in . It is a phasor sum. In 2023 quiz Q6b, adding magnitudes gives the wrong answer by hundreds of volts.
  • Iron loss with instead of . In the simplified circuit is across the input. The PQ 3.29 answer notes this specifically.
  • Forgetting the factor of 3. Both and are per phase in the formula. The output power is usually already a total. The 2023 quiz answers flag this.
  • Copper loss with . includes the magnetising current, so use .
  • Wrong angle sign. A lagging load gives and a leading load gives . When Q is negative (the load generates VAr, 2024 test Q7), the current leads.
  • Line or phase confusion in 3-ph. For star, the phase voltage is . The “required primary voltage” answer is usually the line value, so multiply by at the end.
  • Putting maximum efficiency at rated load. It is where , at , which may be above or below 1.
  • Using in the OC calculation. On open circuit no current flows in the series branch, so use only .

2023 quiz Q7 (quiz, 4 marks). Short-Answer Questions. Answer the following question using words only (that is, without using sketches or equations). In designing a transformer using a given magnetic core, what is the process for selecting the number of turns on the primary winding for a given primary voltage? Carefully explain the results of using too few turns. How about if too many turns are used?

Solution

Model answer (following the course marking points):

  • The number of primary turns sets the peak flux in the core for a given voltage and frequency, through the back-emf equation. The turns are chosen so that the operating peak flux density is below the saturation value of the core material.
  • Too few turns: a higher peak flux density is needed to support the voltage. The core saturates, the magnetising current becomes very large (and distorted), and the winding may overheat.
  • Too many turns: the core runs at a low flux density, so the core is under-used. The extra turns mean more winding length and resistance, so the copper loss is higher, the efficiency is lower, and the winding may overheat.

Jun24 Q4c(ii) (past exam, 3 marks). Answer the following questions using words only (that is, without using any sketches, drawings or equations).

  1. Consider a transformer operating from an AC supply. Carefully explain what are the main types of losses in the transformer, how are they modelled in the simplified equivalent circuit, and how do these vary with output power. [3 marks]
Solution
  • Copper (winding) loss: resistive heating of the primary and secondary windings by the load current. It is modelled by the series winding resistance (the primary resistance plus the referred secondary resistance). Because it depends on the square of the current, it rises with the square of the output.
  • Iron (core) loss: hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the magnetic core, caused by the alternating flux. It is modelled by the core-loss resistance in the shunt branch across the supply. It depends on the flux density and frequency, which are set by the supply voltage and frequency, so it is essentially constant whatever the output.
  • Hence at light load the iron loss dominates, at heavy load the copper loss dominates, and the efficiency is greatest where the two are equal.

N5. Short answer: no-load current and the Prac 2 evidence [4 marks]. In words only:

  1. Why is the input current of a transformer not zero when its secondary is open-circuited? [2]
  2. In Prac 2 the open-circuit current rose from 0.04 A at 100 V to 0.66 A at 240 V. Explain why it rose so much more than the voltage. [2]
Solution

  1. The core has finite permeability, so a magnetising current is needed to supply the mmf that sets up the core flux. In the circuit this is the current through the magnetising reactance, and it lags the voltage by nearly 90°. The changing flux also produces hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the core. These need a real-power component of current, which is modelled by the core-loss resistance. Together these make up the no-load current, which is mostly reactive.

  2. The peak core flux density is proportional to the applied voltage. Near rated voltage the core approaches saturation, and its permeability falls sharply. A much larger magnetising current is then needed for each extra increment of flux, so the magnetising reactance falls (from about 3980 Ω to about 366 Ω in Prac 2). The current rises far faster than the voltage and becomes distorted. The core-loss resistance changed much less, because iron loss depends on flux density and frequency rather than on permeability.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

TRANSFORMER LOAD / REGULATION / EFFICIENCY (per phase, simplified ckt ref. primary)
 R = R1+R2'   X = X1+X2'   shunt Rc || jXm across V1 (input)
 Star: V1 = VL/sqrt3, I1 = IL     Delta: V1 = VL, I1 = IL/sqrt3   (assume star)
 V2' = VL,rated/sqrt3 /_0         S = P/pf  or  S = sqrt(P^2+Q^2)
 I2' = S/(3 V2') /_ -acos(pf) lag, + lead   (Q<0 => leading)
 V1 = V2' + I2'(R + jX)     PHASOR sum -> rectangular -> polar; line = sqrt3|V1|
 Regulation VR = 100(V2NL - V2FL)/V2FL = 100(|V1| - |V2'|)/|V2'|   (V2NL' = V1)
   check: |V1|-|V2'| ~ I2'(R cos(phi) +/- X sin(phi))  (+ lag, - lead; lead can give VR<0)
 PCU = 3 I2'^2 R  (use I2', not I1)  ~ x^2 PCU,FL   (x = per-unit load)
 PFE = 3 V1^2 / Rc  (use V1, not V2')  ~ constant, ~ V^2
 eta = Pout/(Pout+PCU+PFE)   or (Pin - losses)/Pin if Pin given
 Max eta: PCU = PFE -> x = sqrt(PFE/PCU,FL); eta_max = x S pf/(x S pf + 2 PFE)
OPEN CIRCUIT (I2' = 0): Z = Rc || jXm; I1 = V1/|Z|; P = 3V1^2/Rc; Q = 3V1^2/Xm
 V halved: I x0.5, P x0.25, Q x0.25, pf x1 (model). Real core: I falls MORE (less saturation)
SHORT ANSWERS
 Cu loss: I^2R in windings, series R, ~ (output)^2.  Fe loss: hysteresis + eddy, Rc, constant.
 No-load I != 0: magnetising mmf (finite mu, Xm, lags 90deg) + core-loss current (Rc).
 Saturation: B ~ V/(N f); near knee mu falls -> Xm falls -> I rises fast, distorted.
